## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Firecrawl
Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Firecrawl provides web, developer, government, and research search, and executes catalogued Alexandria data providers. Use firecrawl_search to find relevant results across the web and specialized indexes; authenticated searches also return matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and provider contracts; firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_scrape with a url retrieves one supplied page. For a programming question, firecrawl_developer_search searches indexed public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and code documentation and returns the matched passages, and skills: "only" narrows it to agent-skill files; firecrawl_search with categories: ["developer"] reaches the same index beside ordinary web results, returning the hits in the web group rather than as passages and offering no skills filter. For a legal or regulatory question, firecrawl_gov_search searches primary law and regulatory material from US federal, state, and local government sources: statutes, regulations, codes, court opinions, and other government publications; firecrawl_search with categories: ["gov"] reaches the same sources in the web group and cannot be combined with other categories. For a biomedical, life-science, clinical, or arXiv literature question, the firecrawl_research_* tools search the paper index, while categories: ["research"] on firecrawl_search filters ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites. Use the firecrawl_research_* tools to search academic and research literature, expand from anchor papers via the citation graph, and read full-text passages from a specific paper. Search and discovery tools are read-only and return ranked results. Billing: web, developer, and research search are billed per request; government search is free; Alexandria discovery (firecrawl_search with sources ["alexandria"] alone, and firecrawl_find_tools) is free; firecrawl_scrape is billed, as a page retrieval in url mode or at each executed capability's listed price in alexandria mode.

## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects, scoped to the
caller's HeyGen account via OAuth bearer token.

## Available Tools

### Feedback
- **submit_feedback** — Submit feedback the user expressed, or a meaningful terminal
  HyperFrames failure observed after supported recovery failed. Use `source="user"` only
  for the user's statement and `source="agent"` for an agent observation. Submit once per
  issue; omit secrets, raw media, and unrelated conversation text. Expected "project still
  building" responses and redirects to local HyperFrames skills are normal product behavior,
  so they are not automatically reported as failures.

### Author / Edit
- **compose** — Author a new HyperFrames project or apply an edit to an existing
  one. Pass `project_id` from a previous tool call to continue editing the same
  project; leave it empty (or omit) to start a new one. Returns immediately while
  the agent runs in the background (typically a few minutes). An optional
  `design_source` argument picks the brand style: a new project defaults to one of the
  vetted looks (`claude`, `blockframe`, or `monochrome`), with `mat` and `signal` also
  available as built-in presets. The compose response names the style that was applied and
  lists the alternatives, so a first video — when the user hasn't expressed a style
  preference — is a natural moment to let them know a different look is one follow-up
  away. On a follow-up edit, leaving `design_source` out keeps the project's current
  style; it's passed on an edit only to deliberately reskin.

### Read
- **list_projects** — List the caller's projects, newest first. Cursor-paginated

  further pagination.
- **get_project** — Fetch a single project by ID. Returns metadata + a

Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the

Abstract
Blood flow-restricted exercise is currently used as a low-intensity time-efficient approach to reap many of the benefits of
typical high-intensity training. Evidence continues to lend support to the notion that even highly trained individuals, such as
athletes, still benefit from this mode of training. Both resistance and endurance exercise may be combined with blood flow
restriction to provide a spectrum of adaptations in skeletal muscle, spanning from myofibrillar to mitochondrial adjustments.
Such diverse adaptations would benefit both muscular strength and endurance qualities concurrently, which are demanded in
athletic performance, most notably in team sports. Moreover, recent work indicates that when traditional high-load resistance
training is supplemented with low-load, blood flow-restricted exercise, either in the same session or as a separate training
block in a periodised programme, a synergistic and complementary effect on training adaptations may occur. Transient

Abstract
The use of whole-body cryotherapy (WBC) for musculoskeletal ailments is growing. WBC, involving brief exposure to
extremely low temperatures, is increasingly used for its analgesic, anti-inflammatory, and antioxidant effects. The paper
examines the physiological impacts of WBC on cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, hematologic, hormonal, and metabolic
systems. Specific orthopaedic applications discussed include its role in the management of fractures, osteoarthritis, osteone-
crosis of the femoral head, osteomyelitis, adhesive capsulitis, tendinopathies, rheumatic pathologies, chronic pain syndromes,
and fibromyalgia. The study also highlights the benefits and drawbacks of WBC, including its potential to improve athletic

18	Abstract
19	Blood flow-restricted exercise is currently used as a low-intensity time-efficient approach to reap many of the benefits of
20	typical high-intensity training. Evidence continues to lend support to the notion that even highly trained individuals, such as
21	athletes, still benefit from this mode of training. Both resistance and endurance exercise may be combined with blood flow
22	restriction to provide a spectrum of adaptations in skeletal muscle, spanning from myofibrillar to mitochondrial adjustments.
23	Such diverse adaptations would benefit both muscular strength and endurance qualities concurrently, which are demanded in
24	athletic performance, most notably in team sports. Moreover, recent work indicates that when traditional high-load resistance
25	training is supplemented with low-load, blood flow-restricted exercise, either in the same session or as a separate training
26	block in a periodised programme, a synergistic and complementary effect on training adaptations may occur. Transient
27	reductions in mechanical loading of tissues afforded by low-load, blood flow-restricted exercise may also serve a purpose
28	during de-loading, tapering or rehabilitation of musculoskeletal injury. This narrative review aims to expand on the current
29	scientific and practical understanding of how blood flow restriction methods may be applied by coaches and practitioners to
30	enhance current athletic development models.

    REVIEW ARTICLE



Where Does Blood Flow Restriction Fit in the Toolbox of Athletic
Development? A Narrative Review of the Proposed Mechanisms
and Potential Applications
Charlie J. Davids1,2,3      · Llion A. Roberts2,3,4 · Thomas Bjørnsen5,6 · Jonathan M. Peake3,7 · Jeff S. Coombes2 ·
Truls Raastad6,8

Accepted: 24 July 2023
© The Author(s) 2023


Abstract
Blood flow-restricted exercise is currently used as a low-intensity time-efficient approach to reap many of the benefits of
typical high-intensity training. Evidence continues to lend support to the notion that even highly trained individuals, such as
athletes, still benefit from this mode of training. Both resistance and endurance exercise may be combined with blood flow
restriction to provide a spectrum of adaptations in skeletal muscle, spanning from myofibrillar to mitochondrial adjustments.
Such diverse adaptations would benefit both muscular strength and endurance qualities concurrently, which are demanded in
athletic performance, most notably in team sports. Moreover, recent work indicates that when traditional high-load resistance
training is supplemented with low-load, blood flow-restricted exercise, either in the same session or as a separate training
block in a periodised programme, a synergistic and complementary effect on training adaptations may occur. Transient
reductions in mechanical loading of tissues afforded by low-load, blood flow-restricted exercise may also serve a purpose
during de-loading, tapering or rehabilitation of musculoskeletal injury. This narrative review aims to expand on the current
scientific and practical understanding of how blood flow restriction methods may be applied by coaches and practitioners to
enhance current athletic development models.

17	The use of whole-body cryotherapy (WBC) for musculoskeletal ailments is growing. WBC, involving brief exposure to
18	extremely low temperatures, is increasingly used for its analgesic, anti-inflammatory, and antioxidant effects. The paper
19	examines the physiological impacts of WBC on cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, hematologic, hormonal, and metabolic
20	systems. Specific orthopaedic applications discussed include its role in the management of fractures, osteoarthritis, osteone-
21	crosis of the femoral head, osteomyelitis, adhesive capsulitis, tendinopathies, rheumatic pathologies, chronic pain syndromes,
22	and fibromyalgia. The study also highlights the benefits and drawbacks of WBC, including its potential to improve athletic
23	performance, recovery, mood, and well-being, while noting risks like frostbite and impaired muscle strength. Clinical evi-
24	dence from various studies is evaluated, revealing a spectrum of outcomes. For instance, WBC shows promise in enhancing
25	bone health in athletes and providing relief in osteoarthritis and fibromyalgia patients. However, evidence for its efficacy in
26	conditions like chronic pain syndromes and osteomyelitis is less robust. The paper underscores the need for further research
27	to establish standardised protocols and understand long-term effects. While WBC offers significant benefits in orthopaedics,
28	understanding its limitations and potential risks is crucial for its safe and effective clinical application.

 GENERAL REVIEW



Whole‑body cryotherapy in orthopaedics: current concepts
Madhan Jeyaraman1 · Filippo Migliorini2                 · Sangeetha Balaji3 · Swaminathan Ramasubramanian3 ·
Tarun Jayakumar4 · Naveen Jeyaraman1

Received: 9 February 2024 / Accepted: 2 April 2024
© The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer-Verlag France SAS, part of Springer Nature 2024


Abstract
The use of whole-body cryotherapy (WBC) for musculoskeletal ailments is growing. WBC, involving brief exposure to
extremely low temperatures, is increasingly used for its analgesic, anti-inflammatory, and antioxidant effects. The paper
examines the physiological impacts of WBC on cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, hematologic, hormonal, and metabolic
systems. Specific orthopaedic applications discussed include its role in the management of fractures, osteoarthritis, osteone-
crosis of the femoral head, osteomyelitis, adhesive capsulitis, tendinopathies, rheumatic pathologies, chronic pain syndromes,
and fibromyalgia. The study also highlights the benefits and drawbacks of WBC, including its potential to improve athletic
performance, recovery, mood, and well-being, while noting risks like frostbite and impaired muscle strength. Clinical evi-
dence from various studies is evaluated, revealing a spectrum of outcomes. For instance, WBC shows promise in enhancing
bone health in athletes and providing relief in osteoarthritis and fibromyalgia patients. However, evidence for its efficacy in
conditions like chronic pain syndromes and osteomyelitis is less robust. The paper underscores the need for further research
to establish standardised protocols and understand long-term effects. While WBC offers significant benefits in orthopaedics,
understanding its limitations and potential risks is crucial for its safe and effective clinical application.

Keywords Whole-body cryotherapy · Orthopaedics · Musculoskeletal conditions · Rheumatic pathologies

  Why Should Athletes Brake Fast? Inﬂuence of Eccentric Velocity
   on Concentric Performance During Countermovement Jumps
                       at Different Loads
             Jose L. Hernández-Davó,1,2 Rafael Sabido,2 Manuel Omar-García,2 and Daniel Boullosa3,4,5
     1

         Purpose: The aim of the present study was to analyze the effect of different eccentric tempos on eccentric kinetics and kinematics
         and the subsequent concentric performance when performing countermovement jumps against different loads. Methods: After
         1-repetition-maximum assessment and 2 familiarization sessions, 13 well-trained participants performed, in randomized order,
         12 sets (4 tempos × 3 loads) of 4 repetitions of the loaded countermovement-jump exercise. The eccentric tempos analyzed were 5
         and 2 seconds, as fast as possible, and accelerated (ie, without pause between repetitions), while the loads used were 30%, 50%,
         and 70% of 1-repetition maximum. Several kinetic and kinematic variables during both phases were recorded by linking a linear
         position transducer to the barbell. Results: The eccentric work was greater in the accelerated condition despite no changes in the
         eccentric depth. The peak and mean propulsive velocities were greater in the as-fast-as-possible and accelerated conditions.
         Correlation analysis showed that, compared with the 5-second condition, the increased concentric performance in the accelerated
         condition was related to the difference in eccentric work performed in the last 100 milliseconds of the eccentric phase (r > .770).
         Conclusions: Contrary to current practices, the current study highlights the need for performing the eccentric phase of loaded
         countermovement jumps, a common exercise performed by athletes for both training and evaluation purposes, as fast as possible.
         This allows not only a greater eccentric work but also improved concentric performance.

         Keywords: stretch-shortening cycle, muscle power, athletic performance, velocity-based training, force–velocity proﬁle

   "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The review addresses recovery after exercise and inflammatory symptoms, not injury rehabilitation or return-to-play decisions. It cannot show that WBC speeds return to sport after injury."
 }

{
 "id": "Q71",
 "sourceFile": "Why Exercise may be Beneficial in Concussion Rehabilitation- A Cellular Perspective.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Why Exercise may be Beneficial in Concussion Rehabilitation: A Cellular Perspective' matches the filename; the text is an accepted manuscript version.",
 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain": "Brain Health & Psychology",
 "domains": ["Brain Health & Psychology", "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport", "Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Rehabilitation"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Narrative review of concussion pathophysiology (ion dysregulation, energy crisis, impaired neurovascular coupling) and of cellular signalling pathways (BDNF, CREB, mTOR, PGC-1a) that mild exercise may influence after concussion. The authors argue that mild, sub-symptom exercise introduced early may support recovery, and note that several human studies infer autonomic dysfunction from proxy measures. The review cites human studies in which absolute rest did worse than usual care with progressive activity.",
 "screeningLimitations": "No systematic search is described, and the cellular mechanisms rest largely on animal and in vitro work that human studies cannot measure directly. The review does not set exercise dose, timing or safety thresholds from outcome trials in athletes.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the mechanistic pathways as proof that early exercise speeds concussion recovery, when the review presents these links as inferred and the dose as needing individual judgement.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2019,
   "citation": "Dech RT, Bishop SA, Neary JP. Why Exercise may be Beneficial in Concussion Rehabilitation: A Cellular Perspective. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2019.",
   "doi": "10.1016/j.jsams.2019.06.007",
   "abstract": "Concussion diagnosis and rehabilitation have become a prevalent area of research, and exercise is now introduced earlier in recovery. This review aims to refresh the knowledge of concussion from a neurometabolic and broader physiological perspective, using gene expression to show why and how physical activity may optimise recovery at the cellular level.",
   "tldr": "Mild exercise introduced early after concussion may support recovery through cellular signalling, but these links are largely inferred. Use the paper to inform research and clinical thinking, not to set exercise doses.",
   "methods": "Narrative review of concussion pathophysiology and the cellular signalling pathways linked to exercise, with some human physiology studies cited. The text does not describe a systematic search.",
   "findings": "The review describes concussion-induced ion dysregulation, energy crisis and impaired neurovascular coupling, and argues that exercise-related pathways (BDNF, CREB, mTOR, PGC-1a) are active in both exercise and concussion. It reports human studies in which autonomic balance is disrupted after concussion and restored over time, and studies in which absolute rest was not better than usual care with progressive activity.",
   "limitations": "This is a narrative review with no described search, and the authors state that most human autonomic data are proxy measures. The text is an accepted manuscript version, so pagination and volume are not printed.",
   "practicalImplications": "Early, mild, sub-symptom activity is supported over absolute rest in the review's framing. The review does not give a dose, duration or intensity, so any prescription needs clinical supervision.",
   "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Not applicable. The paper concerns post-concussion exercise, not training prescription for healthy athletes.",
   "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The review supports introducing mild, sub-symptom exercise early in concussion recovery, not full training. It cannot set return-to-play criteria or exercise thresholds, because it gives no dose-response or athlete safety data."
 }
}

 "studyDesign": "Laboratory / Experimental Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Training & Performance",
 "domains": ["Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Coaching", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Male Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Randomised within-participant laboratory study in 13 well-trained young men who performed loaded countermovement jumps at 30, 50 and 70% of 1RM under four eccentric tempos: 5 s, 2 s, as fast as possible, and accelerated (consecutive jumps). The fast and accelerated tempos gave more eccentric work in the last 100 ms and higher peak and mean propulsive velocity than the 5 s tempo, and the authors report that the accelerated condition's better concentric performance was related to this extra end-eccentric work (r above .77).",
 "screeningLimitations": "This is a single-session acute study in 13 men, and no training adaptation was measured, so it cannot show whether fast eccentrics improve strength or power over time. The accelerated condition used consecutive jumps with no rest, whereas the other tempos had a 3-second rest, so the conditions differ in more than eccentric speed. The sample is resistance-trained men, not described as competitive athletes.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read this as a rule that all loaded jumps should be braked as fast as possible for better training outcomes, when the study measured acute jump performance only and the accelerated tempo also changed rest.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2024,
   "citation": "Hernández-Davó JL, Sabido R, Omar-García M, Boullosa D. Why Should Athletes Brake Fast? Influence of Eccentric Velocity on Concentric Performance During Countermovement Jumps at Different Loads. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2024 (ahead of print).",
   "doi": "10.1123/ijspp.2023-0273",
   "abstract": "The study compared four eccentric tempos (5 s, 2 s, as fast as possible, and accelerated) on eccentric kinetics and kinematics and on the concentric performance of loaded countermovement jumps at 30, 50 and 70% of 1RM in 13 well-trained participants.",
   "tldr": "In this single session, faster eccentric phases in loaded jumps increased end-eccentric work and jump velocity compared with a 5-second tempo. Treat this as a reason to trial fast eccentrics and monitor the result, not as a settled training rule.",
   "methods": "Randomised, within-participant repeated-measures design. Thirteen well-trained young men completed 12 sets (four eccentric tempos by three loads) of four loaded countermovement jumps after 1RM testing and two familiarisation sessions. Barbell kinematics and kinetics were recorded with a linear position transducer, and a two-way MANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc tests was used.",
   "findings": "The accelerated tempo produced greater total eccentric work than all other tempos at each load. Eccentric work in the last 100 ms was greater in the fast and accelerated tempos than in the 5 s tempo at each load. Peak and mean propulsive velocities were greater in the fast and accelerated tempos than in the 5 s tempo. Eccentric depth did not differ by tempo or load. In the accelerated condition, the change in end-eccentric work was strongly correlated with the change in concentric force (r above .77).",
   "limitations": "This is a single-session acute study in 13 men, with no training outcome. {

 "sourceFile": "Why sports should embrace bilateral asymmetry - A narrative review.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Why Sports Should Embrace Bilateral Asymmetry: A Narrative Review' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain": "Training & Performance",
 "domains": ["Training & Performance", "Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Athletic Training", "Sports Medicine", "Coaching", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Narrative review of bilateral (interlimb) asymmetry in sport, covering its occurrence, its relationship with performance, its link to injury, and the effect of training on it. The authors report that asymmetry is common across sports, ages, sexes and competitive levels, is task- and time-dependent and poorly correlated with performance, and that no evidence shows pre-existing asymmetry raises injury risk or that reducing asymmetry improves performance.",
 "screeningLimitations": "No systematic search method is described, so the selection of studies cannot be checked. Many cited asymmetry studies use single tests or test-retest designs, and sport-specific performance assessments are mostly lacking, as the review itself notes. The no-harm conclusion therefore relies partly on absence of evidence.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the review as saying asymmetry never matters, when it says asymmetry is poorly understood for sport-specific performance and that injuries tend to increase it.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2022,
   "citation": "Afonso J, Peña J, Sá M, Virgile A, García-de-Alcaraz A, Bishop C. Why Sports Should Embrace Bilateral Asymmetry: A Narrative Review. Symmetry. 2022;14:1993.",
   "doi": "10.3390/sym14101993",
   "abstract": "The paper critically reviews the evidence on the occurrence of bilateral asymmetry in sport and its effects on sports performance, injury risk and training, and it argues against assumptions that asymmetry is harmful.",
   "tldr": "Bilateral asymmetry is common in sport and does not appear to impair performance or raise injury risk. Asymmetry scores fluctuate a lot, so judge them over repeated tests rather than from a single result.",
   "methods": "Narrative review of the literature on bilateral asymmetry in sport, organised around occurrence and performance, injury, and training effects. The text does not describe a systematic search.",
   "findings": "Asymmetry is prevalent across several sports regardless of age, sex or competitive level, and can appear even in apparently symmetric actions such as running and rowing. Asymmetry measures are task-, metric- and sport-specific, fluctuate in size and direction over time, and correlate poorly with each other and with performance. Injuries tend to accentuate asymmetry, but pre-existing asymmetry has not been shown to increase injury risk. Training programmes can reduce asymmetry, but the review finds no evidence that this improves sport-specific performance or reduces injury risk.",
   "limitations": "The review is narrative, with no described search, so study selection is not reproducible. Sport-specific performance assessments are mostly lacking, and many cited studies use single tests or test-retest data. The conclusion that asymmetry is not harmful relies partly on absence of evidence.",
   "practicalImplications": "Do not treat one asymmetry score as a problem to correct. Because asymmetry measures fluctuate, use group means and repeated measures, and do not assume that reducing asymmetry improves performance or lowers injury risk.",
   "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Asymmetry is common in athletes and the review argues against targeting symmetry for its own sake. Track interlimb differences across repeated tests and judge them against performance outcomes rather than a fixed symmetry target.",
   "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The review notes that injuries tend to increase asymmetry, but it does not show that pre-existing asymmetry raises injury risk. It cannot be used to set return-to-play symmetry thresholds, because it does not test any clearance criteria."
 }
}
